newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Kulikov is hardline career soldier.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Kulikov is hardline career soldier.

text.p: Russia's Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov, appointed deputy prime minister by President Boris Yeltsin on Tuesday, is a career soldier known for his conservative political views and tough attitude to crime.

Last year he emerged as a leading hawk advocating stepping up Russia's military offensive against separatist fighters in the republic of Chechnya. But his approach lost out when the then Security Chief Alexander Lebed successfully negotiated an end to the war.
The dispute with Lebed erupted into a bitter public war of words, leading eventually to two separate defamation court cases which went opposite ways.

Yeltsin appointed Kulikov Russian interior minister in July 1995. During the previous six months Kulikov had commanded the joint defence and interior ministry troops in Chechnya, which declared itself independent from Russia in 1991.

On Tuesday Yeltsin's office announced that Kulikov, a 50-year-old four-star general, would also hold the title of deputy prime minister in charge of the tax police, customs and other agencies dealing with economic crime.
He did not immediately outline initiatives in these areas, although in the past he has advocated stronger efforts in tax and duty collection as a way to boost government revenue.

Former Finance Minister Boris Fyodorov, referring to Kulikov's remarks a year ago that Russia should nationalise some commercial banks, said Kulikov was not likely to make a big impact in tax collection and other economic spheres.

"A person like that who never had anything to do with any financial matters, who is famous for making statements about banks and so on which were ridiculous, I don't believe that this will help really," Fyodorov, now a member of parliament, told Reuters.

"And in any case, my personal belief, even when I was myself deputy prime minister, was that we have too many deputy prime ministers, and then ministers have no role," he said. Kulikov will become the ninth deputy prime minister in the government.

Since the complete withdrawal of Russian forces from Chechnya last month, Kulikov's primary focus has been the fight against crime, which has strangled many sectors of the country's economy since the fall of communism in 1991.
Last week he declared that Russia was winning the battle with crime, citing a 4.7 percent drop in overall crime in 1996 compared to the previous year.
Gennady Sergeyev, a director at Moscow's National and International Security Foundation, which publishes a magazine on security issues, said this decline showed Kulikov's ability as a crime fighter.
"It's a move toward pragmatism and good efficient work," he said of Kulikov's promotion. "The dynamic in the most serious areas of crime is going down."

Many Russians still say crime remains pervasive, and point to a series of high-profile mafia-style killings that are still unsolved despite Kulikov's tough words. And the interior ministry soldiers under Kulikov's command were frequently humiliated by determined but lightly armed separatists in Russia's 21-month war in Chechnya.

Nonetheless Kulikov has risen rapidly in recent years. A deputy interior minister since late 1992, he was loyal to Yeltsin during a failed uprising by hardline parliamentarians in Moscow in October 1993. He held a number of commands in the interior ministry troops since the mid-1970s.

Kulikov is from the Stavropol region, a fertile farming area in southern Russia. He is a graduate of the Vladikavkaz Higher All Arms Command School and the prestigious Frunze Military Academy as well as the General Staff Academy.
